speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as today has been set apart for the official observance in Canada of His Majesty's birthday I am sure

it will be the wish of all hon. members that an expression of their good wishes be extended to His Majesty, King George VI, from this House of Commons. I have had a word this morning with my friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and he and I have agreed on a resolution which we are sure that hon. members will be pleased to support. I would suggest that after the motion has been put by His Honour the Speaker, and any other hon. members who may wish to speak to the motion have addressed the house, we should signify our approval of it by the singing of God Save the King.
The motion, seconded by Mr. Bracken, is as follows:
That an humble address be sent to His Majesty, King George VI, in the following words:
"To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We,-the members of the House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled, desire respectfully to extend to Your Majesty, on this day set apart for the celebration in Canada of the King's birthday, our loyal greetings and heartfelt good wishes. We pray that Divine Providence may continue to guide and protect Your Majesty and that you may be given strength to meet in the future as you have in the past the great responsibilities of your high office."

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Oppositioh):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXTENDING GREETINGS AND GOOD WISHES TO HIS MAJESTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to associate myself with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in this resolution. I am pleased also to associate the party I lead with the good wishes it expresses to His Majesty the King.
This is a resolution which does not need the support of argument in order to secure what I trust will be the unanimous approval of this house. The crown in all parts of the commonwealth has come to mean to us more than a hereditary position, more than royalty, more than kingship as we have known it in the past. The crown has come to mean a continuing democracy, no matter how often governments change, and no matter what partj is in power. Members of the commonwealth may differ in many things, but there is od' thing in which they do not differ, and that is in the respect we have for the person of His Majesty the King and the high regard we have for the crown as we have come to know it. I am very happy indeed to have this opportunity of associating this group with the spirit of the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FURTHER LIST OF ARTICLES AND SERVICES REMOVED FROM CEILING AND RATIONING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that effective today a further list of articles and services has been removed from price ceiling and rationing controls. The list is much shorter and less important than at previous stages of the decontrol programme. The main groups are, first, certain products which it is desirable to remove from control now because of seasonal factors; secondly, a number of metals which show signs of having settled at price levels on world markets substantially above those prevailing in pre-war years; and, thirdly, restaurant meals.
The most important foodstuffs released from price control are dairy products of all kinds, including butter, cheese, evaporated milk and ice cream. These products are now at their seasonal peak of production and price ceilings can therefore be removed with minimum danger of significant price increases. At the same time butter is removed from the list of rationed foods.
Honey, being subject to the same seasonal factors, is removed from both price control and rationing. All jams, jellies and marmatdes are also being derationed but price controls are being retained on strawberry and raspberry jam and any jam containing strawberries or raspberries.
Eggs were removed from price control several weeks ago. Because of good supplies it has now been decided to remove ceilings from poultry and poultry products of all kinds. Canned soups and salt are also released from price ceilings.
With respect to clothing, home furnishings and household equipment and supplies, the items removed from control are of relatively minor importance, and I shall not take the time of the house by listing them.
All agricultural equipment and supplies remain under the ceiling, with the exception of brooders, incubators and other poultry equipment for which the current season is past. Hay, which will soon be at its season of high production, is free from control.
The new order provides for the removal of only three items in the list of construction products, namely, hardwood lumber and plywood made wholly of hardwood and hardwood veneers. This action has been taken, first because practically all end-products have already been removed from control, and, second, because increased production in the United States, accompanied by some recession in United States prices, is now reducing the cost of hardwood imported into Canada. Mill-work of all kinds remains under control.
In the metals field, the new order removes from control lead, copper and zinc, leaving under control only primary and secondary tin and alloys containing more than 95 per cent tin. World prices of lead, copper and zinc appear to have settled fairly steadily at levels considerably above pre-war. Since practically all the end-products which embody these metals have already been removed from control, this appeared to be a logical time to complete the process of decontrol of these items.
The only other important change is to free from control the supplying of meals and refreshments in all public eating places. The government has had to recognize the fact that during the past few months most of the costs which enter into restaurant meals either have been decontrolled or, as in the case of meat, butter, sugar, shortening and rents, have had authorized price increases. The government considers the time now appropriate to take this further step.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: ADMISSION OF DISPLACED PERSONS FROM . EUROPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the house an order in council, P.C. 2180, relating to immigration. The order provides for the immediate admission to Canada of S,000 persons from the displaced persons' camps of Europe.
The'5,000 individuals to be covered by this order will include those displaced persons who have already been admitted. They need not be relatives of residents of Canada. The new order is designed as a further Canadian contribution to the solution of the general problem of the displaced persons.
In the selection of displaced persons, priority will be given to those persons who have skills and aptitudes which will make them capable of absorption in industries where there is a reasonable guarantee of steady employment. In the light of the existing housing situation, priority will also be accorded to single persons.
In discussing this matter in the past the Canadian government has taken the attitude that we would be prepared to do our full share, along with other countries, whenever an international agreement could be reached on the disposal of the persons in these camps. With that end in view, we have supported the work of the international committee on refugees and have taken a prominent part in the negotiations leading to the establishment of the international refugee organization.
We had hoped and expected that more rapid action would have been possible in connection with the organization of the I.R.O. and that this would have facilitated the early conclusion of an agreement on the disposal of the displaced persons. However, one delay after another has occurred and it now looks as though it would still be a matter of some months before the I.R.O. is established and is able to work out the terms of an international agreement.
Rather than wait for the initiation and the completion of the negotiations for a general attack upon the refugee problem, the government has decided to make this initial contribution to the solution of the problem.
The number of persons admitted as a result of this initiative will, of course, be deductable from any general quota that Canada agrees to accept following the international discussions on this subject.
As has been repeatedly pointed out, the greatest present difficulty in the way of a major immigration movement to Canada is the lack of shipping. I am now glad to be able to report that the government hopes to be able to arrange for the conversion for immigration purposes of a vessel received on reparations account from Germany. In addition, we are continuing our efforts to obtain more space for immigrants on vessels under the control of the I.G.C.R. or provided by the British ministry of transport.
With regard to the plans for the selection, transportation and distribution within Canada of the	persons	covered	by	the new order,it has been arranged that the handling of these matters outside Canada will be under the control	of the	immigration	branch of	theDepartment of	Mines	and	Resources;	andwithin	Canada,	under	the	control of	the
Department of Labour. In carrying out its work of selection and transportation the immigration service will be assisted by representatives of the Department of Labour, and in arranging for the distribution of the new immigrants throughout Canada the Department of Labour will receive assistance from the officers of the immigration service within this country. It is expected, for example, that the immigration buildings in several of our larger cities will be used as distribution centres in which the new immigrants may be initially received, and from which they may be sent on to their ultimate destination.
The government does not, of course, consider that this initiative will meet the full Canadian responsibility in relation to the displaced persons. We do believe, however, that it is a contribution towards the solution of this very grave problem and is a recognition of our moral obligation to contribute to a solution.

speechtext: Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved the third reading of Bill No. 253, to make provision with respect to forces of the United States of America when visiting Canada and with respect to the exercise of discipline and to the internal administration of such forces.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this measure before it is given third reading. I am not going to deal with the principle of the bill, because that was settled on Friday when we voted for second reading. When the bill was being considered in committee of the whole a statement was made that to me is somewhat disturbing. The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe), in discussing certain aspects of the bill, made this statement:
I propose to ask the minister a question which he may or may not care to answer. I believe that it should be asked and that some definite statement should be made with respect to it. This committee should be informed as to how many United States troops are in this country at the present time. We should know what they are doing in Canada and what their disposition is, that is to say, in what parts of the country they are at the present time.

Visiting Forces
That is at page 3876 of Hansard. In reply, on the same page, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) mentioned that the number of United States troops stationed in Canada was not very large, and that wherever they were stationed they were fewer in number than the Canadian troops who were with them. His statement was:
They are less numerous than our own personnel. It is by design and arrangement that they are kept less numerous than our own. That is the way in which the policy is being carried out.	.
But in regard to United States troops in other parts of Canada the minister said:
There are a few others at other places, but I would not feel at liberty to disclose that information without conferring with the chief of staff and ascertaining whether it would be proper to do so.
It seems to me an amazing state of affairs that a member of the cabinet, asked a question in this house, cannot answer that question until he refers the subject matter to the chief of staff. That sort of answer might have been satisfactory when the country was at war, but certainly it is not a satisfactory answer at the present time, when the country is at peace. I believe-and in this matter I think the precedents in British countries hold with me-that the members of this house should be informed not only as to where foreign troops are, when they are on our soil, and what they are doing, but also where our own troops are, when they are under arms, and what they are doing. That should be so in time of peace. If we are secretive about these matters surely we are bound to create suspicion not only in our own country but outside as well. So I would suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that even now, before this bill is given third reading, he should give a full and complete answer as to the number of United States troops in this country, where they are stationed and what they are doing. Parliament is entitled to that information, and nothing less; and I believe that in the interests of world peace and the elimination of suspicion in these affairs the answer should be given before this bill receives third reading.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The reason for my statement that I would wish to Confer with the chief of staff before answering that question was not that I wish to have the opinion of the chief of staff about it; but as it had to do with the presence here of men in uniform from our neighbour to the south, I wished to be informed by him whether it might be embarrassing to him in his relations with them to have that information published. The hon. member will realize that these matters are not of very great consequence at the present time,
because there are only very small numbers who are cooperating; but I did not feel at liberty to answer without being sure that when the arrangements had been made for a few men to come to such and such a place, it was with the express or implied understanding that the particulars could be made public. I think the hon. member will agree that we are under some obligation of courtesy in that regard, and it was for that reason that I stated perhaps in general terms what I should have stated a little more precisely, that I wanted to be sure there would be no violation of courtesy in giving that information.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
May I just add one word to what my hon. friend from Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has said. It is not a matter of courtesy. May I say to the minister that we are prepared to extend all the courtesies possible to our great American neighbour. But throughout the ages-at least ever since the execution of Charles I-the right of parliament to know what troops or armies are within the borders of the country, and under whose command they are, and what they are doing, has been a fundamental principle of our British parliamentary practice. It is not because we wish to be discourteous to our. great neighbour to the south, but rather because we believe this parliament has a right-indeed a duty-to inquire into the movement of foreign troops in this country in peace time-and I say "in peace time" because when we are at war and allied with another nation, circumstances are entirely different-we have a duty, I say, to ask what troops are on our soil. We have a duty in relation to our own troops to see to it that no outside individual or group shall have control in our own country. If it is true that this parliament has entire control of military arrangements within our own country, then parliament should know exactly what troops, other than our own, are on the soil of Canada at a given time. That is the point at issue-not	the matter of courtesy or
discourtesy.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has referred to the time-honoured rule which, he says, is observed in the British parliament, that information as to the number of troops in the country must be disclosed at all times.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: To parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, to parliament. I can refer my hon. friend to a refusal to indicate to the British parliament the number of

Visiting Forces
British troops in Great Britain, which was given, by their minister of defence on March 4, 1947, as reported at page 43 of their Hansard. I have looked into this matter and I can refer the hon. member to a number of other answers in the debates of the House of Commons at Westminster in the course of which ministers of the crown have refused, on the ground of public interest, to give information as to the detailed disposition of their own forces in Great Britain or outside Great Britain.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is familiar with the discussions which took place before the united nations as to the desirability of full disclosure by all nations of information of military value; and he knows how far that suggestion got before that body. He must know that in these matters, if you give all the information you have to other countr.es, you have very little chance of getting any information in return. I will be frank with the house and say that in this instance the information is not of any genuine military significance, because the numbers are so small and the operations are of such a routine character that they would not be of any great significance to any country.
We hope that the international situation will not deteriorate; we hope that it may be possible to exchange information on terms of complete and guaranteed reciprocity with all countries. But we are not certain that that day will come. Until it does come we do not feel it is in the interests of Canada or of the defence of this continent to establish the precedent of making disclosures not only to members of parliament-because there is no difficulty about that-but to the public and to other nations, of the detailed disposition, purpose, location and numbers of our forces or those of any friendly country within our boundaries, because of the significance that might be attached to changes and developments that might be made.
The situation as it exists today is, as I say, not at all significant or serious. But let us suppose, for example, that three more weather stations or five more loran stations are built, and let us suppose that the number of men serving those stations, partly Canadian and partly American, has increased. That can be played up in this or in other countries as a dangerous and threatening sign, whereas everyone in this country knows that it would be nothing but the most reasonable step in the defence of our own country and to prepare us for any emergency that may arise.
These matters of defence have changed greatly since the period between the two wars.

Now we have inventions like radar, loran and inventions of other types which are of use principally for defensive purposes. Their location and number may be of some interest, and until we can secure an exchange of information on a guaranteed reciprocal basis we do not propose to give that information away to anyone who wants to get it. But as for hon. members in the house, let me say that we should be glad indeed to give them the fullest possible information as to the situation.
What I have said does not apply to the total of forces or to matters which are of common interest and common knowledge in Canada. But we do not believe it is a good thing to give information as to the disposition, location, purpose and strength of these forces in detail, not because of what exists today, but because of some significance which may be attached to changes in the future-and which almost certainly would be attached, judging from our experience.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Vancouver-East deplored the debate; and I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs went some way in agreeing	with	them.	I	too	would	like	toexpress regret at	some	of	the	things	said	in
the debate; but I would call attention to the fact that many of them, which I believe many of us would regret, were occasioned by the amendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) representing the C.C.F.
When later the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said	that	some	of	the	things	said	indebate did	not	represent	the	point	of view
of parliament or of the country, I must say the question arose in my mind whether some of the statements of the hon. member for Regina City, as reported at pages 3795 and following, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre at page 3835 and the hon. member for Swift Current at page 3846, represent the views of the C.C.F. That they did not represent the views of parliament or of the country I am convinced, but I think it is of interest to learn if they did represent the views of the C.C.F.
As a further word in conclusion I would point out that some thirty speakers took part in the debate, of whom thirteen were members of the official opposition and nine were members of the C.C.F. while only six speeches were made by representatives on this side. Of those six, two speeches were made by the minister who introduced the bill, and one by myself in explanation of some of its features. It cannot be said that this debate was in any way occasioned or carried on by members

Visiting Forces
on this side, it can be said to the contrary that more than two-thirds of the time of parliament was taken up by representatives of the opposition.
In our view this bill was not a bill of great significance. It was designed to enable Canada to extend in peace time a privilege that it had been found useful to accord to the troops of the other country in war time. It does not infringe on the sovereignty of Canada or on the jurisdiction of our courts. It simply gives visiting forces tc our country the privilege of trying their own men for offences under their own military law. It is a privilege extended by the United Kingdom to the United States and Canada. It is a privilege extended by the United States to the United Kingdom and Canada. It is a privilege extended already by Canada to the rest of the commonwealth, and it seemed to us to be a reasonable provision and in accordance with our common interests that we should extend the same privilege to the United States that they had already extended to us.
Hon. members have spoken throughout this debate as if the advantages of our common participation in joint defence1 in accordance with the arrangements announced by the President and by the Prime Minister on the 12th of February were entirely one-sided. The arrangement was spoken of as if Canada were the only beneficiary. This arrangement was made in the interests of Canada, of course, but it was made by the United States in the interests of the United States. It is in our common interest, and that is why it was made. Further, the cooperation extended under the arrangement is by no means one-sided. On account of the fact that the United States has some twelve times our population and many times our wealth and many times our power, she naturally has the most to contribute. But it is by no means a one-sided arrangement, and I can assure the members of the house that we intend to have this arrangement carried' out, so far as lies within our power, on a reciprocal basis, by means of which we would give to the United1 States the full advantage of such inventions, discoveries and works as we have-there is much we can claim to our credit in these fields-and we shall also engage with them in common measures of joint training and the like.
Hon. members spoke as if it were contemplated that there would be large numbers of United States troops drilling and training here. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has made it clear that that is not contemplated at the present time at all. This is entirely, I would say, at the staff, liaison,
testing and experimental level. So there is no considerable group of United States troops in Canada and no group of Canadian troops in the United States at the present time receiving training for training's sake, that is, which will be of primary value because its primary purpose is directly to increase their military skill. This is an extension of the kind of arrangement friendly countries have carried on throughout the ages, the exchange of staff information, the exchange for training purposes of staff, the exchange of matters of common interest of one kind or another. No other two adjacent countries, I think, on the face of the earth have ever before had such close and intimate relations as the United States and Canada, and have such common interests in their common defence. It is because of that that this arrangement was made, born of the statement of the President and the Prime Minister in 1938, carried through in the declaration of Ogdensburg on August 19, 1940, and the basis for so much of the allied cooperation which contributed to victory. It seemed to us that this arrangement should be carried on in peace. It seemed to us to be the merest act of common sense in the common interests of two good neighbours.

speechtext: The section is intended to mean "at any time during the last month." Perhaps I should say it was my own fault.

At the same time, the C.C.F. group did not know that this bill was coming up. They took the same meaning as we did from what was said by the minister on Friday night, where he pointed out that the government would like to follow the order of the three bills mentioned, and that probably this one might be available. But it was not available then, and did not become so until Saturday. If it could be held over for another day I would certainly appreciate it, because some hon. members would like to give some thought to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I dislike forcing the bill, but the Prime Minister has said time and again that the house should be ready to take up any matters on the order paper. While giving notice the night before or, as in the present instance, two or three days before, is an act of courtesy-and desirable, of course -it must be remembered that this will be a broken week. We shall have the visit of President Truman and, while I do not wish to make any personal appeal, I should point out that I have more legislation to bring in. If we could make headway in the committee stage today, I would appreciate it.
I shall give this undertaking, that if there are any sections hon. members feel they would like to have stand, where there is some point to which they would like to give further consideration, we could allow those sections to stand and proceed with others. In that way we could make headway today. I put that suggestion forward for the consideration of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I point out what I said on Thursday night when announcing the business of the house. I said:
Tomorrow, if the budget bills are ready I might ask the consent of the house to have them introduced and read for the first time, kept over the week-end for consideration and discussed fully next week.
So that no member can complain of any lack of notice in regard to this bill.

That did not mean on Monday. The worst of this is that it destroys the confidence which ought to exist in this house. The minister speaks of being burdened. The members are burdened too, and extremely heavily, and they have a right to consideration. I will say no more about the matter, but I think this is one of the basest tricks that I have seen perpetrated in the house since I have been here.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

Income War Tax Act
On section 2-Security in lieu of interest or dividend.

I wish to say a word mainly by way of repetition of what I said at the resolution stage.
I must confess, since the minister has not seen the light up to now, it may be that we cannot persuade him to see it today. It does seem to me that a clause of this kind, which really undertakes to say that a document does not mean what it says it means, is unfortunate. Take the case of a man with a $100 bond which has been in default, let us say for ten years, as may well happen. If the arrears are all paid up in one year and the bondholder is taxed on one year's income that seems a hardship, and if it can be avoided I think we may fairly call it an injustice. If the minister is sure that it cannot be avoided I must confess that that would impress me a good deal, but I earnestly suggest that parliament should not pass legislation like this which says that a document, "notwithstanding the form or legal effect of the transaction," is to mean something entirely different from what was intended and from what it says it means. The effect will be to incite people, indeed drive people to various ways of attempting to get around such a provision. I am sure that the minister never in his legal practice did that, but there are other lawyers who do. I suggest also that the people who can take advantage of it are those who are well versed in these matters, not the ordinary man on the street. Without labouring the point or holding up the committee, I would ask the minister once more, is it not possible to do what I believe justice would suggest and as has been done in several other cases, to spread this over several years; in other words, to recognize that a situation of this kind can be a hardship, and an injustice if it can be avoided?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did give consideration to my hon. friend's point, but there are grave difficulties in doing what he suggests. I do not believe there will be any substantial hardship, because, as he will notice on looking at the rates of tax, the brackets are fairly wide. Between $3,500 and $5,000 the rate is the same, twenty-two per cent, and it would take a substantial holding of bonds and fairly substantial arrears of interest to put the man into a higher bracket. Suppose a man did get $25 on a $100 bond, and suppose he had 1,000 of them; he would get $250, and that would not push him into the higher bracket unless he was on the edge of it. I think, upon reflection, my hon. friend would agree that
with the fairly wide brackets before the income tax rates change there is not much likelihood of any real hardship. A man would have to be a substantial holder of the particular bonds m arrears and would have to receive a very large amount of arrears in order to change substantially his rate of tax.

I should like to add my word of appeal to the minister to that offered by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. I offer it, in the first place, on the ground of fairness. The arrears presumably have accumulated over a period of years and some rights are to be given by way of recoupment for the losses sustained over that period. Yet the proposal is that the rights, whatever they may be worth, shall be taxed in the first year. So, first on the ground of fairness, I urge the minister to reconsider this provision.
In the second place, may I urge, as did the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, that when a provision smacks of unfairness, as this will to many people, the temptation to find ways and means to get around it is very strong. It would be a bold member who would undertake to say that there will not be cases where the incidence of the tax as contemplated by this section may not be defeated by transfers in anticipation of the issue of such rights. When the tax smacks of unfairness from the beginning the minister would, I think, have to admit that many to whom he referred as being on the borderline of a higher tax bracket will be tempted to find ways and means of evading the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section in terms is substantially analogous to a section contained in the British act, which has been there for some time. I think it is a desirable section to have in our law because there was a loophole there which could lend itself to serious abuse. There are not a great many of these refinancing obligations. The one case that brought it to my attention was that of Abitibi Pulp and Paper Company, where there were substantial arrears. I do not think I could agree to amend the section this year to allow any such arrears to be spread over a period of years. As I said in answer to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, I do not believe there will be any substantial injustice done, but I will give further consideration to the question and when we bring in our new bill which will be effective for the 1948 period, if I find that a real case can be made out for my hon. friend's suggestion, we can include it in the new bill.

I thank the minister and would add just one
Income War Tax Act

word. As the hon. member 'for Winnipeg North Centre said, we often ask for things and do not get what we want the first time or the second but, if we keep on, we sometimes get it. The minister spoke of the unlikelihood of a payment of this kind forcing a man into a higher bracket. That may be true. But even a man with an income of $2,500 is going to pay twenty-five per cent upon any excess over $2,500. I am not going to labour the matter further. I thank the minister for promising to give it further consideration.

I realize that such a provision is in all the other acts and I realize the difficulties. A case that affects a great many citizens of Toronto is a refunded municipal bond that has been in arrears over a number of years and then the arrears are paid in one fell swoop. If that is paid in a lump sum it certainly puts the taxpayer into a much higher bracket. He could get around this by selling his bonds before payment is made through the municipal refinancing. If he sells his bonds, it is a capital gain and. is not taxable. If he holds on to his bonds and accepts the refinancing, then it is income. It is a difficult point; nevertheless consideration should be given to it. A man holding a bond of some of the municipalities which were in default in the last depression, having bought the bond at par or nearly par, finds that it is now selling at a considerable discount. The principal may be selling at $40 or $50. He has received no income from it for a period of six or seven years, which is a serious setback so far as income is concerned. Then he gets the whole thing at one fell swoop and is taxed at a much higher rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably not, because the brackets are so wide.

Two things mitigate
against the cases I have in mind. First of all, the man holds security for a number of years and does not get anything from it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And therefore pays no tax.

That is so, but if he bought the security for income he gets nothing from it for years. I believe some of these bonds were in default for six or seven years. He gets nothing from it in that period of six or seven years; therefore he is penalized in those years. That is his bad judgment. The government cannot do anything about a man's judgment; but he is definitely penalized. Then he gets the income all at one time and is again penalized for those six or seven years during which he has been able to receive no income. He gets it two ways. First, he does not get his income and, then, he gets it in

one block and is taxed, despite the fact that in the bill this year the brackets are much wider than they have been. This is one of the things that must be given real consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says that the problem is one that is pretty difficult; but he will appreciate, as will other hon. members of the committee, that the refunding which takes place from now on will be on a descending scale of taxes. The tax which will be paid for the whole of the bond on the accumulated income will, in all probability, be at a substantially lower rate than he would have paid had the interest been paid during the war when rates were at a much higher level. On balance, I think it will be found that the actual tax contribution on the accumulated arrears of interest will be less than the aggregate of the tax which would have been paid had the interest been paid as it went along and included in the individual's tax returns. In most cases I think it will be found that that is true.

I see the point with a decreasing scale. Let us pray that we have not seen the last of decreases in income tax; let us hope that it will be an annual thing and that every year we shall have less and less income tax. But my point is this: two things mitigate against it. One of the things is that municipal bonds-and there will be difficulties with municipal financing-are going to run into difficult times when municipal authorities ask for supervision or are unable to meet their interest charges. At that time the bonds will sell at a discount. Because of the government's policy, the hope that the bond will come back and that the interest will be paid on the years when the municipality is not able to service its bonds, has in many cases kept the security of the municipality at a reasonable level. But because of the continuation of this policy, we see bonds selling at forty per cent or fifty per cent of their par value, and men will hesitate to buy them and therefore support the market because, if the bonds are made good and the arrears are paid, or a substantial payment is made of the arrears, they will be taxed for it all in one fell swoop. In my opinion that will make municipal financing just that much more difficult. At the moment municipalities are able to borrow money at low interest rates. Their credit is extremely high, but there will be difficulties ahead, and this is one of the difficulties that must be foreseen.

In
the explanatory notes and in the remarks of the minister the words "funding" and "refunding. are used. I wonder -whether this position

Income War Tax Act
will apply to a mortgage. Take a mortgage that had been - in arrears for a considerable period of years and a new mortgage was given to include both principal and interest. First, would the interest be taxable in that year? Second, take a case under the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, where default has been made, and after going through certain proceedings, the mortgage reverts to its former position before action is taken. There would then be a large accumulated fund and interest which would come due. Would that apply in the same way here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To answer my hon. friend's first question, this section does not relate to mortgages as such. It relates only to security, funding securities in the nature of stocks, bonds, and so on, although the language is broad enough to cover securities in the sense that a mortgage is a security. That has always been the rule. Where a mortgage that is in arrears is paid up with arrears of interest and a new mortgage given consolidating the principal and interest, then I would think the portion of the new mortgage which represents the accumulated arrears of interest would be income in the year in which the new mortgage was taken. Therefore the answer there is in the affirmative.
How do you know the new mortgage would ever be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
How do you know that
the new Abitibi bonds will be paid? You take them. The creditor takes them in satisfying the interest and the claim in the same way that stock dividends and other dividends under the Income War Tax Act are income in the hands of the person who receives them. He is getting only a piece of paper, it is true, but the earned surplus of the company is capitalized; the shareholder gets new stock certificates for the arrears of dividends, and that has been income in the year in which it is received.

I
am sorry to hear the minister say that, because I am more convinced than ever that there will be all sorts of ways and means found to evade it.

There is one word in this section which calls for a word of comment from the minister. In line 24 we find the following: "The value of the security or other right." In the case of a security that is of doubtful value, how is the department to determine the value? Will it be determined in the face amount of the substitute or
supplemental security? Otherwise it will be a vague and uncertain kind of taxing provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend who is a capable lawyer knows, value is a question of fact, and sometimes it is extremely difficult to ascertain just what the real value, the current value of a particular piece of property, is. I think the best line to follow is to use the word "value" in the act and, in the case of dispute, to leave it to the courts to determine what that value is. That is the usual procedure in any other case where there is a dispute as to value. Under the succession duties law, for instance; there may be another adjective attached to "value"; I do not remember. The essential word is "value". I take it that the practice would be for the taxpayer to report the funding security and to place a value on it. If the income tax collector felt that the value was too low he would assess for the difference. If the taxpayer were dissatisfied with the income tax collector's assessment he would appeal in the usual way, and in the final analysis, if it were sufficiently important it would have to go through the exchequer court and perhaps the supreme court. I see no other satisfactory way of putting it in the law. It would be dangerous in this case, as in most others to attempt to define what is value in the case of a fairly wide range of assets. I think it would be better to leave it to the appropriate forum, namely the court. That is what the courts are for in cases of disagreement.

I think the minister will agree that the first duty of parliament in writing taxation laws is to be just and fair. The second duty of parliament must be to achieve clarity and certainty in the taxing law. Here we have a provision which, according to the minister's statement, is bound to provide much administrative difficulty and to give rise to many disputes between the taxpayer and the taxing authorities. Undoubtedly it will be the occasion of many appeals. I wonder if the result is justified by the end that the minister is seeking to attain here.
What the minister has just said buttresses the argument of those on this side of the house who have been talking about the unfairness of a taxing measure which arbitrarily imposes a tax in the year in which the obligation is created regardless of whether it may or may not ever be satisfied and regardless of the period of time for which the obligation in redemption or liquidation of which it is given has arisen. Are not those factors which ought to weigh seriously in the minds of members in legislating for a new tax of this kind?
I urge that it is a contradiction in terms for parliament to legislate an income tax act which

Income War Tax Act
says that something shall be income which may never come into the hands of the individual except perhaps as a piece of paper, which may never be translated into dollars and cents. It seems to me that by every canon of interpretation of income tax law, by every recognized rule, by the golden rule of interpretation, barring some special statutory definition, income is only- that which is received. It becomes income only when it is actually received.
Here parliament is being asked to say that when a man has been given a piece of paper which is payable over a period of years, which in fact may never be paid, it shall be considered as income, and be taxable in the year in which it is handed over by the debtor to the creditor. I have heard the minister's explanation, in which he has been fair with the committee, but it does seem to me that in treating such rights as income a taxing measure such as the minister has described is manifestly unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I say, I am fully conscious of the difficulties which are involved in this section. I gave it a tremendous amount of consideration when the Abitibi funding operations were on, for reasons which I think will be appreciated. At first I issued a statement that they would be taxed in the hands of the person who received them. Then I realized that that would be retroactive legislation which would be unfair, and I said it would be effective only from the time the budget was brought down. It is inevitable that we should have this sort of thing when we are dealing with intangible property rather than cash. It would be manifestly unfair to the taxpayer to use the term "face value".
I really think it is better to leave the matter for determination by the courts if necessary in the event of dispute. I venture to say that in ninety-nine cases out of 100 there will be no difficulty. In the case of publicly listed securities there are quotations on the market and those will establish the value for tax purposes. I imagine the difficulty will arise in the case of a private concern where there is' no readily available market. Those cases are not very numerous, comparatively speaking. There it would be a matter for determination, in the first instance, by agreement if possible between the taxpayer and the income tax authorities and, in the event of dispute, for determination in the usual way.
As I say, I am conscious of the difficulties that are inherent in this thing, but I have not been able to find any better solution. As I pointed out before, this is the method which has been followed in Great Britain for a number of years and, so far as we can ascertain, it appears to have worked reasonably well.

As a matter of clarification and'administration, do I take it that if somebody happens to have securities in which the principal and interest are blended, it is perfectly clear that the principal comes out first? If the value were such as to show nothing over and above the principal, there would be no tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a legal question involved there which I do not know that I would care to give an opinion on off hand. I am thinking of the rules in the province of Quebec with respect to the imputation of payments when there is a payment on account of principal and interest. It might be that there would have to be some apportionment between the capital obligation and the interest obligation. Our rule in Quebec is that if payment is made and there is no designation of payment by the debtor, it is paid, first, on account of interest and second, on account of principal. I do not know what the rule is in the common law provinces.

I would have hoped that the minister had stopped with 'his first answer, but he evidently thought it required clarification. It seems to me that hardship will occur if that point is not made clear. Does the minister not think that should not be made clear?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Apparently there was a case in Toronto where there was a large mortgage with substantial arrears of interest. A new mortgage was issued consolidating the principal and interest and then calling for the payment of principal and interest over a period of years. That case went .to the exchequer court and certain rules have been laid down with respect to apportionment, but I could not give them. Again that is a matter of law. There is no definition in the act.
We are making law now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section will not make income of anything that would not be income at some time under some other provision of the act.

I do not want to be too persistent, but if there is any doubt about that I should like to ask the minister whether he agrees, as I think he does, that perhaps we are imposing a considerable hardship upon people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The language of the section is quite specific; it says that payment must be made in lieu of payment of or otherwise

Income War Tax Act
in satisfaction of an interest, dividend or other debt. That is the rule laid down here.
Section agreed to on division.
On section 3-Cooperatives.

If I interpret this section aright it provides for something for which the cooperative union asked in their submission to the government in April. I commend the minister for introducing this section, and I am sorry to know that no more submissions by the cooperative union have been adopted by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are two others.

I intended to make a speech in support of the argument of the cooperative union, but in view of the work ahead of parliament I shall desist. I should like to ask the minister a question about the procedure in connection with the taxation of cooperatives. A few weeks ago I received a number of letters from cooperative associations in my constituency with respect to a directive that had been issued in connection with the filing of returns by cooperative associations.
I do not think I can do better than read one of those letters which contains the wording of the directive and also an argument as to why the directive should be abandoned. This letter is addressed to me under date of April 28, 1947, by the Eston, Cooperative Association Limited, and reads:
We have been advised of a recent directive of the Department of National Revenue,_ Ottawa, in regard to taxation of patronage dividends, reading as follows:
"Where a consumer cooperative sells to customers both 'cost of living goods' and 'cost of production goods' the onus is on the cooperative to make the division of the patronage dividend and show the amount that applies to each class of dividend on Form P.D. 5 supplementary otherwise, if no division is shown, the whole of the patronage dividend will be taxed in the hands of the recipient, instead of just the portion which applies to 'cost of production goods .
Our board of directors are convinced that it is impossible to comply with this directive, in some instances the co-op manager would know whether an item was "cost of production goods or "consumer goods," but in most cases it would be impossible for him to know. For instance, how could he know whether a pound of nails went into a dwelling or into a pig pen? Or, whether a gallon of gas was used in a tractor, ear, washing machine or stove? Groceries could even at times be "cost of production goods" if used to feed hired help.
We feel that .the task of complying would be impossible, but if the manager should attempt it, the members could rightfully ask, "Who gave the co-op manager the right to say what is my income and what is not?"
We would ask you to use your influence to have this directive cancelled and let each taxpayer decide what part of his patronage dividend is income, and what part is not. _
Hoping you will be able to help to straighten this out, we are,
Yours respectfully.
Eston Cooperative Association, Limited, per V. M. Hanson, Secretary.
The question I wish to ask the minister is whether he has received many complaints and whether he has considered the cancellation of this directive, because I think it is oppressive and almost impossible to be complied with.

Before the minister answers, may I associate myself with the question asked by the hon. member for Kindersley. I should like to remind the minister that I took up with him by letter this question along with several others affecting cooperatives, after having had the same point drawn to my attention, I wrote to the minister and received his reply of May 16, 1947. Since it is not marked "private", I presume there would be no objection if I at least gave the effect of it. I am glad to find that the minister said:
I am, nevertheless, giving consideration to the possibility of making changes in the act or m the regulations which will relieve cooperatives of tax for periods prior to January 1, 1916. It it is possible to make this change, notice will be given when the bill to amend the income tax act is brought d-own.
I read that into the record in order to ask the minister whether he is now in a position to say whether that change will be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The change to which the hon. member has referred is made by this section. That is the change which the section is intended to accomplish.
The point of the change was to relieve them of responsibility before 1946.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is done in this section. Although the section may look a little bit technical in its drafting, I can assure my hon. friend that is done or will be done when this section becomes law. There is no tax on cooperatives for 1946.
To answer the hon. member for Kindersley, I am not familiar with the problem which he has just raised. It sounds to me as if it were an administrative decision or ruling in the Department of National Revenue. I will see that his remarks are brought to the attention of the appropriate officers. I shall see whether the ruling to which the hon. member refers can be amended or varied in order to meet the point he has raised. I myself am not familiar with it. After listening to my hon. friend, I do not believe it is a point which would require legislation in order to accomplish what
Income War Tax Act

he has in mind. That is not to admit, of course, that it is, of necessity desirable. But I do not think we should require an amendment to the act in order to allow that apportionment to which he refers to be made. I can assure my hon. friend that we would not need law to do that.

A letter which I wrote to the minister, to which his letter was in reply, had to do with the same matter to which the hon. member for Kindersley was referring, and the objection which I was making was that the income tax return required cooperatives to show "what portion of refund was on 'living expense' and what on 'production expense' The letter to me went on:
All this is entirely new and applies to 1945 business altho' paid in 1946.
The point made by my correspondent was this. After he had closed his books for 1945 and had not.kept books in such a way that he could say what portion was on one and what was on the other, he wanted to know how he could be expected now, in 1947, to go back to 1945. Business done in 1945 was reflected in the 1946 tax which was payable on April 30, 1947. I had intended to cover both points in my letter to the minister, and when I saw his answer saying that the matter would be considered and possibly a change would be effected in this bill, I thought he was referring to both points. It does seem to me that to make a distinction between what portion of a payment is on "living expense" and what portion is on "production expense", is really more than an administrative matter. Would that not require a definition? Could that not be covered by a definition in the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not too familiar with the particular practice to which the two hon. gentlemen have referred, but the officials assure me that this is a matter for administrative determination. The question of not being taxable in 1946 is taken care of in the amendment which is introduced in this section. The other question, I am told, does not require an amendment. The situation, as I understand it, is this. I think I made the statement in the house that a dividend from a consumer cooperative was not taxable, but a dividend from a producer cooperative was. There are some cooperatives which are both producer and consumer cooperatives. That is, I believe, correct. The difficulty arises in apportioning the patronage dividend which is declared and paid, as between the consumer part of the business and the producer part. That does not require specific law. That is a question of accounting practice, administrative determination, or whatever y.ou like to call it. Possibly 
the Department of National Revenue makes certain rules on apportionment and those rules may not be-and I say "may not be"- soundly based. But they can change them if they are not. That is the point which I think my hon. friend has in mind.
It is a matter entirely for the Department of National Revenue, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is an administrative decision of the Department of National Revenue in accordance with the facts; it is made according to accounting principles, on whatever the facts show.

I should like to ask the minister one question while he is dealing with cooperatives, and I ask it purely' as a matter of information. It has to do with the great confusion which exists among cheese factories as to whether they are to be taxed in 1947. In eastern Ontario there are a great many of these cheese factories; some are incorporated as cooperatives, some as joint stock companies, and some have really no legal incorporation of any kind. But roughly, the cheese factory consists simply of a number of farmers who have joined together for the production and manufacture of cheese and butter; and after the deduction of costs of manufacture and other running expenses, the remainder of the money on hand is divided among the patrons according to the number of pounds of milk they have sent in during the year. I think it would be helpful if the Minister of Finance or his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, could make some kind of statement as to these various cheese factories. I would point out to the minister that the only official in the factory who is paid is the president, who is generally also the secretary and treasurer. They have the idea, perhaps wrongly, that they are now to be taxed and be burdened with complicated returns, deductions and things of that kind. If the minister could make some simple statement, I am sure it would be very much appreciated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is perhaps right; if it were possible to make a statement which would cover all cases, it would undoubtedly be helpful. I am told that the conditions vary so much, as my hon. friend has indicated, in these different cooperatives that it is hard to make a short, simple statement covering them all. If they are a corporation, then, of course, they are subject to tax in 1947, the same as any other corporation. If they have paid out patronage dividends these are deductible as an expense before arriving at the net taxable income. My colleague the Minister of National Revenue points out that, in answer

Income War Tax Act
to a question asked two or three months ago by my hon. friend, he gave this reply. I do not know whether the committee wants me to repeat it, but the question was:
Will the Minister of National Revenue in the near future make a statement in the house outlining the interpretation of the deputy minister of taxation of the 1946 amendment to the Income War Tax Act in regard to cooperatives in so far as the amendment applies to cheese factories in the province of Ontario which operate more or less on a cooperative basis?
The reply, which appears at page 261 of Hansard, was:
In view of the fact that cheese factories conduct their affairs in varied manners, it is not possible to state specifically which sections of the 1946 amendments to the Income War Tax Act, in so far as they refer to payments to customers, would be applicable to any particular cheese factory. The manner in which a cheese factory would be taxed would depend on whether it was wholly a cooperative, partly a cooperative or a purely private operation. In the case of any particular company it would, of course, be possible to give a specific answer privately to the taxpayer.
If it is not a corporation, incorporated under the cooperatives act of Ontario, if there is such an act, or some other act, then, of course, it would not be taxable at all as a corporation. The individual members would be taxable on any profits they made; but I am advised that it is almost and in fact quite impossible to give a general statement with respect to cooperatives other than a statement such as that given by the Minister of National Revenue, because of the wide variety of conditions under which the cheese factories operate; some operating as cooperatives, some more or less as cooperatives, as my hon. friend has said, and so on.

I want to point out that none of these cheese factories, as far as I know, pay any patronage dividends or anything of that kind. The only income a patron receives from his cheese factory is his share of the total proceeds which he receives, figured on the number of pounds of milk he sends during the year, after all the usual running expenses have been deducted. No one receives any dividend on his stock, or anything like that.

I think the hon. member has raised an important point. There is a great deal of confusion in my own riding. A number of farmers, without actually incorporating, lend money to a cheese factory and claim to hold shares. But they and others send milk to the factory, and they are. paid for their milk on this basis. The cost of production is estimated and deducted from the receipts, and the remainder is distributed
to the farmers in accordance with the volume of milk delivered, with no provision whatever for the financial interest of anyone in the company. They are in a sense a cooperative, but they get no dividends or premiums; what they receive for their milk is entirely commensurate with the volume they bring in, and has little connection with the capital of the concern. In other words, no matter how many shares a farmer may hold in the enterprise, he does not get a bit more per pound of milk than the farmer who does not hold any shares. Many farmers have had to do this sort of thing in order to keep their factories operating. Some factories even pay a small rate of interest on the money lent by way of shares, but many do not even do that. There is no incorporation. They are cooperatives in the sense that the total cost of production is deducted from the bulk receipts, and the remainder is distributed on the basis of the amount of milk sent in. If the minister could make a statement dealing with a case of that kind I believe he would enlighten a great number of farmers in this community, and probably would end a good many of the difficulties of the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I followed my hon. friend's remarks with some interest. As he stated the case, it seemed to me that this would be a sort of voluntary association, not incorporated. The individuals would be subject to tax on the receipts from their produce, but they would not be subject to the provisions of the Income War Tax Act with respect to the tax on corporations, which is the tax imposed on cooperative corporations the same as on all others.

But they have been
assessed for tax as an association by the Department of National Revenue. Really they are only partners; they are not cooperatives in the strict sense of the word. I believe the farmers will very much appreciate being notified of what the minister has just said.

I wish to express once more my regret that there is no increase in the exemptions, which are indicated here as
Income War Tax Act

$1,500 in the case of a married taxpayer, and so on down the line. I believe the present exemption of $100 per child is also too low. If one has a taxable income within the meaning of the act he is allowed an exemption of $100 for each child under the age of sixteen; and, in effect, by this legislation you have taken away whatever benefits a family enjoyed when it first received the family allowance. Once the child passes the age of sixteen, the family allowance stops, and of course the exemption is then increased to S300. That would be perhaps nearer the cost of maintaining a child than the exemption of $100 plus whatever the family allowance amounts to. There is some attempt at grading the expense, as I see it, because, in effect, an infant gets an exemption of about $160.	Then, as the
child gets on toward sixteen years of age, the exemption works up to $196, when it reaches the maximum of $300. I believe the minister has set that figure too low.
There is one matter I should like to mention in connection with this question of exemptions, and I ask the minister's permission to introduce it here. I refer to the exemptions allowed to a class of people who receive a great deal more by way of platitudes than by way of income, and I have in mind our teachers. They are subject to the same taxes and exemptions as other wage-earners, with the exception that they are not permitted deductions for what I think are necessary expenditures to stay abreast of their profession and keep up with educational procedure. I have particularly in mind such things as summer-school courses, which it is most necessary for teachers to take from time to time, and the acquisition and maintenance of an educational library. These things are not considered by taxation officials as allowable professional expenditures in the case of teachers, and it seems to me that the department should reconsider its attitude in this regard. Representations have been made to the government from time to time, and I believe there is a definite injustice.
Before I resume my seat, I should like to mention a matter in connection with the expense allowance permitted in certain districts for the necessary use of an automobile in the conduct of business; and I wish to refer the minister to a particular case in which I had an opportunity to see the documents. This refers to a real estate salesman who required the use of an automobile in 1944. Because there was gasoline rationing at that time apparently he was permitted to put in a claim to the extent of 6,000 miles of travel at 4| cents a mile, making a deduction of $260, from which was deducted a quarter of 
the complete cost of the allowance, leaving his net deduction the sum of $202.50. That was the amount set down as his gasoline and car operational expenses for the year, despite the fact that there were vouchers in support of his claim which, in this instance, amounted to $328 for the year.
It seems to me that the treatment given by the minister's department to people who must necessarily use their automobiles in business differs considerably from the treatment the government gives its own civil servants who use their own automobiles and receive a mileage allowance running from eight cents to eleven cents, depending on the area in which they travel. If it is justifiable to give a higher allowance to civil servants who use their automobiles in their business, the same consideration should be given others, particularly those in receipt of incomes as modest as the one to which I have just referred, and which affects one of my own constituents.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on section 4 of the Income War Tax Act, exemptions and deductions.

In view of the current increase in the cost of living-and I do not think anyone would care to say that the increase has ended-will consideration be given to increasing the exemption for dependents, say children?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think consideration will be given to that this year.
Was consideration given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Consideration was given to the whole picture, but the increased cost of living was not taken into account. The exemption structure has been worked out over a considerable period of time, and more effective relief can, I think, be given in the tax rate than by raising exemptions for children or for married status or raising the exemption to a level below which the income is not taxable.

If S300 a year was a fair deduction for children in times when the cost of living was not as high as it is today I suggest that, to maintain parity of treatment between those who have children dependents and other classes, some adjustment upward should be made in the exemptions for dependents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That point could, of course, be argued. But these exemptions must be looked at over the longer period. The cost of living varies from time to time. It is true that in recent months, perhaps years, it has been tending upward, but I would not be prepared to say that is a permanent trend, for we may well see some reduction in the cost of living. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would prefer to finish this bill first.
- Has the minister anything further to say by way of explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is an intricate provision and difficult to explain. The provision of the law, as my hon. friend knows, is this, that special inventory reserves could, under the Excess Profits Tax Act, be set up out of liability for excess profits tax and then be charged back at a later date if and when inventory losses were established. As we shall see under the Excess Profits Tax Act, any amount left over must be charged back anyway. If a loss is established in, let us say 1946, and an inventory loss taken in the same year, a portion of that reserve can be taken and charged back in that year, thereby converting the year into a year of profit. To take a specific case, if the operating loss were $10,000, including inventory losses, and a reserve of $40,000 had been set up, then $40,000 could be taken off and credited to profit and loss account, which would result in a profit for the year of $30,000. Under the averaging provisions in section 5(1) (p), that $10,000 operating loss could be taken back into the previous year, could be averaged with the previous year; and, suppose the previous year had shown a profit of $50,000; that $10,000 loss could be deducted from the profit so that a profit of $40,000 would be shown for that year. This would mean that the income tax branch would reopen the assessment for the previous year and, in averaging the loss, would make a new assessment for income tax. That is perfectly all right so far as income tax is concerned. But the loss so established should not be taken into account when taken back for excess profits [DOT]tax purposes, because the reserve has already been taken as a deduction and should not again be taken in the averaging provision.
The purpose of this amendment is to assure that the loss which is taken back and averaged with a previous year will be for income tax purposes only, not for excess profits tax purposes. When you take back the figure and average for excess profits tax purposes jmu must take into account the figure arrived at for excess profits tax in the year in which the reserve is utilized in order that
it will not be taken twice. That sounds complicated but that is the exact position. The reason for inserting the provision in the income tax act is that the act as it now stands provides that for the purpose of computing excess profits tax and liability for excess profits tax the net income for income tax purposes will be taken. That is perfectly all right except in cases such as we are now considering where a special reserve is utilized for arriving at profits for excess profits tax purposes but not for income tax purposes. The purpose of the amendment is to assure that the reserve will be utilized for the purpose here but should not be utilized twice, averaging the excess profits tax in a previous year where the benefit has already been taken. As my hon. friend knows, there is not a self-contained definition of income in the Excess Profits Tax Act. The definition in the income tax act is incorporated by reference into the Excess Profits Tax Act.

The last lines of paragraph 3 of section 4 read as follows:

These words are not new; they are in the present act, but I should like to ask the minister if, in point of interpretation by the department, the word "adoption" is construed as applying only where an adoption order has been made under an adoption act of one of the provinces, or whether "adoption" in fact in such case that the taxpayer stands in loco parentis to the dependent is sufficient without a formal adoption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised that is adoption in fact, and that the exchequer court has recently so held.
