speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
One of the provisions of this section is to fix the exemption levels at $1,500 and $750. It is not my purpose at this time to discuss these levels as such, for we have alreadj' expressed our views with regard to that phase of the matter. I should like to know whether there has been any change made with respect to the point at which family allowances are recovered. My point in asking this is that last year some portion of the family allowance was recoverable in the case of a married taxpayer earning $1,300. As a matter of fact, at that point a married taxpayer with up to three dependents had to pay back five per cent of his family allowances. A

Income War Tax Act
married taxpayer earning $1,400 and having even as many as four dependents, according to last year's rates, paid back ten per cent of the family allowance that he received. If that has not been changed, my point is that the effect is to establish two different exemption levels, and it provides, as from these levels, two different scales of taxation.
It is generally understood that a married man with four children would have an exemption level of $1,900. That is true, if the $1,900 is income that he earns at his employment; but if a married man with four children is earning only $1,400 and receives family allowance, let us say, of $312 for his four children, putting him up to a total of $1,712 I contend that he pays what amounts to a tax of ten per cent on the $312 family allowance that has been given to him. May I make the point again? Here is a married man with four children whose total income is only $1,712, but because $312 of that is family allowance he pays tax on all he has received over the level of $1,400; he does not get the benefit of the $1,900 level that is accorded to the average taxpayer. I am anxious to know whether a change has been made in connection with this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The recovery provisions do not apply any more since January 1, 1947. Since January 1, 1947, the structure is pretty fairly simplified. If a man has children of family allowance age he receives his basic exemption of $1,500, of course, for being married. Then, if he has four children of family allowance age he would be entitled to another $400 exemption, $100 per child and, as my hon. friend has pointed out, that would give him a total exemption of $1,900 before he pays any tax. But he receives his full family allowance for the four children and there is no refund whatsoever, no matter what his income may be.
In the other case cited by my hon. friend, a total income of $1,400 with four children, he pays no income tax, of course, because he is below the exemption limit, and he receives his full family allowance. On that basis, with four children, he could have an income up to $1,800. .

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, up to $1,900 if he had that income; that is correct. But if his income were $1,400 he pays no tax; he is below the exemption limit, and he does not need any children's exemption because his income is below the limit where it would be of any use to him. He receives full family allowance, whatever it may be, with the four 83166-251
children; it is not taxable income, of course, and there is no question of any refund in that case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am very happy to hear that. Can the minister tell me how this arrangement was made? Was it by an administrative order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; it is in the law; it has been there since last year's budget. It started on January 1, 1947. It was as a result of careful study and the combining of the family allowance and the basic exemption. That was one of the reasons why it was felt necessary that everyone who had children of family allowance age should apply for and receive family allowance in order that everyone would be on a uniform basis of exemptions and that there would be no question of * these refunds or reductions of family allowance because of the income tax scale.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, family allowance is now treated as income and one does not pay tax on it unless the family allowance puts him above the normal brackets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Family allowance income is tax exempt income in the hands of anybody. If I have an income today of $1,900 and I have ten children, all of whom are eligible for family allowance, I get the family allowance for the full ten and I get my regular taxation exemption of $1,500 plus another $100 for each child. As a matter of fact, that would be $2,500 in the case I am giving. It would be a total exemption of $2,500 plus non-taxable income of whatever the family allowance would amount to for the ten children.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: So that the provisions that applied to the taxation year 1946 do not apply to 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do not apply now. Since January 1, 1947, the new system has been in effect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is fine.

Before section 4 is disposed of, I should like to direct attention to one important matter. Residing in Canada we have quite a number of married men who entered this country as immigrants during the late twenties or at other times. Owing to adverse economic conditions which prevailed during the thirties, these persons were unable to contribute substantially, if at all, toward the maintenance of their families which were domiciled outside this country. With the commencement of the war and the general improvement in economic conditions, these persons, while able to contribute toward the support of their families, were not permitted

Income War Tax Act

to do so because of war conditions. However, since the war, government regulations have permitted the transmission of funds abroad to provide for the wives and children; yet today we find that the department is refusing to recognize these persons as married persons. Even where receipts are produced showing that amounts of money are being forwarded for the support of these families, they are still not regarded as having married status. Does the minister regard that as completely fair; if not, what does he intend doing about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought I must be dreaming or something, but that is the purpose of the present amendment; that is what the section is being amended to provide for. I thought for a moment that my hon. friend was suggesting some other case. The proposed amendment to the section provides that the restriction which formerly existed, that they must reside in any part of His Majesty's dominions or a country contiguous to Canada, or, residing elsewhere, be a subject or citizen of a country associated or allied with Canada in the conduct of the war, shall be removed. All that will be necessary under this bill will be for a person in Canada claiming married status to establish that he has a wife living, let us say in Czechoslovakia, and is remitting funds to support her.
Will this apply to all countries or just to those countries which were allied with us?,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will apply to all countries. We are removing the restriction now in the act that it must be His Majesty's dominions or a subject or citizen of a country associated or allied with Canada in the conduct of the war. There is now no limitation.

When we were in committee on the resolution I brought to the minister's attention what I considered to be discrimination against domestic servants in the maritime provinces. At that time I pointed out that a domestic servant in New Brunswick was obliged to add to his or her income $26 a month for board and lodging, while in the province of Quebec a similar domestic servant was obliged to add only $15 a month to his or her income. If my information was correct this meant that in certain instances a domestic servant in New Brunswick would have to pay income tax-this would apply also to the other maritime provinces-while a domestic servant in Quebec would not be obliged to do so.
At the same time I also brought to the minister's attention that porters, waiters and certain other employees on the Atlantic division of the railroad were obliged to add $300
to their incomes in lieu of tips, while in other railway divisions the same employees did not have to add this $300 to their income when making out their income tax returns. The minister stated at that time that there was no discrimination, but he said he would look into the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the Minister of National Revenue has information on that matter and one or two others that were brought up. I do not know the wishes of the committee, but I had thought that, after we had concluded the specific sections of the bill, the minister could then deal with the questions raised by my hon. friend. I think the point he raised could appropriately be discussed under this section and he may prefer to have the information now.
It makes no difference to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps we might as well give it now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
With regard to the first matter brought up by the hon. member, the answers which we have received from the several districts are to the effect that the allowances vary from $180 to $360 a year. The reports indicate, however, that there is no hard and fast rule and that every effort is made to take into account the type of home in which the domestic is employed and the nature of the board and lodging received. The amount of the wages and the nature of the board and lodging received really have to be taken together. The employer, in dealing with the employee, sometimes will offer a nicely furnished independent room, and a more than ordinarily luxurious table may be kept. A domestic may accept a lower monthly wage for steady employment in such a household than he or she would where the accommodation is on a minimum basis and tenure of employment less secure.
In general, the amount added in the majority of cases tends to run about $20 a month, and in the average case this is rather low having regard to present-day conditions and cost of living.
It is the belief of the administrative officers that this is a matter which should continue to be left to the judgment of the assessors and officials in the district offices familiar with the individual cases, and that to set any hard and fast rule may impose a hardship in some instances and allow unduly favourable treatment in others. Living conditions in various provinces and homes in Canada vary considerably and the assessors are required to make a fair-minded appraisal of the facts in each individual instance.

Income War Tax Act
The second question which the hon. member asked had to do with tips paid to railway porters, stewards and waiters operating between Halifax and Montreal. I think the claim was that m the maritimes S300 was added, but that nothing was added in the case of the Montreal district. The consensus of the reports which we have received from our district offices throughout the country is that the cases are dealt with on their merits, much depending on the nature of the run upon which the employee may be engaged. A waiter attending people in the luxury class travelling, say from Toronto to Vancouver, would undoubtedly receive much more in the way of tips than a waiter on a train, say from Montreal to Sherbrooke or Quebec, where only the casual businessman would have a meal in the club car. In this, as in other matters, the heads of the district offices attempt to deal on a factual basis, which means that they make due allowance for differences in circumstances of the individual taxpayer.
The problem of income by way of tips, however, is difficult. It is in the category of income of which there is no record and in all cases our assessors have to be governed by some attempt to determine probabilities.
Their general attitude where they set arbitrary allowances for tips is to set them safely on the low side. Three hundred dollars a year for a waiter with a run on a transcontinental luxury train would be about $1 a day or thirty-five cents per meal hour. I do not think anyone with any familiarity with the facts would complain that this was excessive as a yearly basis for tips which such a man might receive.
Do I understand that the amounts charged for board and lodging would vary in different cases in New Brunswick, or are they the same in all cases?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: It would vary in different cases, but the average is approximately $20 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps that could be
answered a little later on this evening. In any event, it would be covered by an administrative regulation.

time prescribed. They have no record of having imposed any penalty for non-compliance and feel that the fine referred to in the letter must apply to some matter other than tax deduction.

I should' like to raise again a question that I referred to during the resolution stage with respect to people living in northern, out of the way areas. Could they have transportation expense to a doctor included in the exemption? I have experience of cases which are sent south, say from the Queen Charlotte islands, to Vancouver. They are dismissed from the hospital but must live in a rooming house near the hospital in order to go there for treatment each day. Yet that expense is not exempted, and it is making it absolutely impossible for fishermen, for instance, who live in villages at out of the way points along the coast, to take treatment. They would like to go to live in Vancouver but it is economically impossible. I bring this to the attention of the minister in the hope that he can do something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand my hon. friend's question-and I remember when he asked it before-it was to extend the application of extraordinary medical expenses to the cost of board and lodging when, of necessity, people have to come from remote points to get hospitalization. I promised to give consideration to that, and I will do so, but it is a big question. You cannot just say you can give that exemption without consideration, because you have to see where these things lead you. This is importing an unusual principle into the income tax law when it is suggested that we allow board and lodging as an expense. I can see that it would be an expense which relatives would necessarily be put to, or even the people who were going down to undergo treatment. But I do not believe that I should be prepared to introduce an amendment in this year's bill without giving the matter much more consideration than I have been able to do up to the present time. I doubt whether the present

provisions of the act are broad enough to cover it. I think it would require an amendment to the law.

I should like to ask the minister a question w'hich affects married veterans attending university. Take the case of a veteran attending a university, who is married and is drawing only $60 a month allowance, but is not drawing the extra allowance for his wife, and his wife is working. Suppose she is earning $2,000 a year. In that case is the wife entitled to a $1,500 exemption? If, during the summer months, the husband earns, say $500, what would be the amount which would be deducted from the wife's exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case given by my hon. friend, I am advised that the wife would be entitled to take the married exemption of $1,500. The $60 a month, or whatever it is which the veteran would be receiving-that would be a matter of $720 a year-while it is not taxable in his hands, is taken into account in calculating the wife's married exemption; and it would probably have the effect of reducing it by the amount which it exceeds $250. The extra $500 odd would reduce the wife's $1,500 exemption by a corresponding amount. It works in just the same way as it would if the husband were in receipt of the income and the wife in receipt of the smaller revenue.

Has there been some change, or do I understand the minister correctly? Suppose the veteran gets $600 or at the rate of $60 a month. Do I understand the minister correctly as saying that from the $600 he deducts $250, and the remainder over $250 is deductible from the wife's exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. There was one point I overlooked in answering my hon. niend's question. If the veteran earned extra money during the summer, that would have to be included as well in calculating the wife's final exemption.
Then I would suggest to the minister that, at that rate, this $60 a month which is a part of the reestablishment credit, is really being taxed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, there is no tax on it.
It is the same thing. His wife has to suffer. It is deducted from her exemption for married status.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the amendment
carry?

Just a minute. I should like to ask the minister a further question. Take the case of a child attending university. Is that child still allowed to earn up to $400 during the summer and the parent still get exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct, if the child is under twenty-one years of age.

Under twenty-one, of course. Then I suggest to the minister that it is hardly fair that the child can earn up to $400 and the parent can still get exemption, while the husband who is also in this case going to school, will really have part of his reestablishment credit deducted from his wife's exemption of $1,500. I think the minister will agree that is hardly fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Logically, of course, when providing the $250 rule in the case of a married woman we should have done the same thing in the case of dependents who are going to college; but I am advised that would make it unnecessarily complicated, and it was decided to leave that just as it was. There was one point I overlooked, which I should have mentioned: that the wife gets the $1,500 exemption on the assumption, of course, that she is supporting the husband.
She is assisting to support her husband.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right; but the whole basis of the marital exemption for anyone, as I have had to point out time and again here, is that the spouse who is getting the exemption is supporting the other spouse. If the husband or wife, as the case may be, is only partly supporting the other consort, then the exemption is correspondingly reduced. That is the basis of the exemption.

But I would point out that there seems to be a certain amount of discrimination against the veteran who is getting $60 a month. You take the various other benefits allowed under war service act, or under the Veterans' Land Act. A veteran who takes up land under that act gets extensive benefits by way of loans for the purchase of stock, and so on, which he does not have to pay back; and then a certain amount is written off. In that case there is no question of any part of the grant being taxable in any way. But here is a veteran attending university; he is really being taxed on his reestablishment credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no tax on the reestablishment credit of the veteran. If the veteran is not married he supports himself, presumably, out of the allowance he gets under
the provisions relating to veterans attending university. He gets his university fees paid, and works in the summer. If he has a wife who is able to earn income which is taxable, then he lives a little better than the veteran who is single; but the wife is entitled to an exemption as a married woman only if she is supporting her husband, if her husband is dependent upon her for support. So that there is no tax on the husband's allowance as a veteran. As to there being any discrimination as between the veteran attending university and the veteran going on the land, I think anyone who knows, as my hon. friend does, the monetary value of a college education will realize that the money cost is very much more than in almost any other branch of veterans benefits, because a man who is capable and qualified to go to university can get the equivalent of five or six or seven thousand dollars in veterans benefits over the course of his university career.

I would not altogether say that. It depends upon the length of time the veteran spent in the armed forces. If he has been in the army for only a year he gets credit only for twelve months at university.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That applies to the other benefits also.
Yes; and it is only in a few cases that a veteran who has been in the army for only six or twelve or eighteen months is going to have his tuition and fees paid for the full course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right; but the point is that proportionately the veteran who is able to qualify to go to university gets a higher benefit than almost any other class of veteran.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As to potential benefits for boys going to university, there is discretion in the minister to continue their courses into post-graduate work; so that those benefits can be much greater than the $2,300 odd they get under the Veterans Land Act.
I did not intend to refer to that point, but I think the minister will agree that those benefits are extended only to those who come within the seventy-five per cent average.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

And I believe they are very few.
The question I wished to ask the minister was in relation to a farmer or other person who might have a woodlot on which the lumber had been growing for a long period of years. We know that during the war,

when prices were high, much of tihis lumber was cut; and many farmers and others who owned these small woodlots were very much surprised to find themselves taxed for the full amount they received for their lumber. If they realized five or six or seven thousand dollars they had to pay t'he tax on that amount as income for that particular year. This was felt to be quite a hardship. I believe the question of exemptions comes in here again. As I have said, this lumber was growing for perhaps twenty-five or thirty years; and if the amount realized had been spread over a number of years, these men would have received the benefit of the exemptions for each year. I believe what applies to lumber applies also to a man who sold his herd of cattle. The amount he received from the sale of his herd, which had taken a good many years to build up, was taxed as income for that one year. I should like to have the minister's opinion on these points.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is asking a large question which, of course, involves a difficult administrative decision as to what is capital and what is income. If the taxpayer in question were a farmer, I do not know whether lumber could be included in the averaging which is now available to farmers.
It is not a yearly crop.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is true. Certainly if he had any losses he could average them against it. I am afraid I could not give my hon. friend an offhand opinion as to what the ruling of the income tax branch would or should be in the case of a sale of wood or lumber. Obviously there is a point at which the line has to be drawn between capital and income; and I would think the case is analogous to that of the basic herd, wthich we are discussing here.
I think there is some unfairness.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a point where I can see there would be room for unfairness.
Does the minister wish to leave all the questions raised by the hon. member for Battle River until the end?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was what I thought. I have a memorandum in which I have covered the various points the hon. member raised, and I thought it might make for more orderly discussion if I handled them all, say on the last section.
These income taxes are, I assume, a method of attaining some end. What is the aim, the end in view in connection with these income taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The main end in view is to help pay the country's bills.

Why do you tax the people ; and if you do tax the people, what is it you desire? Do you desire paper money, bills; or pieces of metal, coins; or do you desire signs or symbols, units of account which are dollars? I should like the minister to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, we are not too particular. We want something the public will take in payment of the country's liabilities.

Then would the minister answer this question. Why are the people taxed? The people are neither the creators, the source of paper money, nor the source of coins, nor the source of these signs or symbols which are dollars. Would the minister tell me why the income tax officials do not go to the source of money to obtain it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not able to answer my hon. friend's question. My own view is that the only source from which we can collect taxes is people.
I did not hear what the minister said; he was talking away from me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; I was addressing the Chair. I said that from my experience the only source of taxation is people. You cannot tax inanimate things.

Why tax at all? You see, I do not create any money except my own turkey money. The source of money is definitely not the people, and I claim that all taxation is downright robbery. I am just waiting until the people are sufficiently awake to this robbery that they will demand the immediate resignation of all officials who are imposing these penalties upon them.
I spoke to the deputy minister of taxation on the sixth floor of this building, and I introduced him to my wife as the commander in chief who engaged the troops to rob us on our own farms of money which we did not create and which we require for production. I claim that today production is being deliberately restricted, because I know that on my own farms, if it were not for this income tax I would wire my sons and tell them to get busy and produce to capacity. Yet on my own farms, where I can produce 500 to 1,000 hogs a year, not a single hog is being born because of this downright robbery. I can

Income IFar Tax Act
produce a ton of butter at present a month, but I am not producing a single pound of butter for sale. Agriculture throughout Canada can produce all the wool we require if we could cut out this damnable robbery. I claim the Minister of Finance will be held personally responsible for this insecurity he has created.
This robbery must cease. I am telling my people, and telling them bluntly, that until they revolt against this robbery they will never obtain their freedom. And I claim this income tax is introduced and imposed upon the people for no reason other than that of bringing them down to the status of slaves.
The minister does not know why people are taxed, when all the money, all the figures in the world can be created at will. I rode down on the train with a couple of senators, and I asked those old senators why in the world they permitted this robbery to continue. They said to me, "Where is the money coming from?" "Why", I said, "do you really want to know?" "Yes," they said. "Well now", I said, "don't resist what I am going to tell you. You sit right there and I will tell you where the money comes from." Then I pulled a bill out of my pocket, and I asked them, "What is this?" They said, "This is ten dollars." I said, "It is not ten dollars, because it says right on the bill 'will pay to the bearer on demand ten dollars.' "
I say, if we want bills, we can create all the bills we want, all we desire. All we have to do is to get the authority and call up the British American Bank Note Company. I believe that is the company which printed this one I have in my hand; yes, I see it was the British American Bank Note Company. They make them. This is a perfectly good bill; it is perfectly good money; there is nothing wrong with it. The British American Bank Note Company is an absolutely reliable company.
On a question of privilege, when an hon. member produces a document, does he not have to table it?
I am perfectly willing to have :t tabled.
Page boy!
Table it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Sticky fingers.

I said to these senators, "All we have to do is to instruct this reliable company to print all the bills we require, if it is paper money we need. They can bring them to us by the bale. All we have to do is to ask them how much they charge for running these through." Then, if they say they charge
a thousand dollars, I can peel a thousand dollars off the bale and pay them. The remainder costs us nothing.
Then, when it comes to coins, I say we can produce all the coins we want, absolutely free. If a lump of gold, silver or copper, or whatever it may be, were brought and placed upon my desk, and if I had the authority I could obtain it all, absolutely free. I do not know how I can get it otherwise, except absolutely free. I can say to the man, "Here, take $10,000 out of the bale, and I will buy it." The bills cost me nothing. The man would say, "Well, I am not going to lug around a bale of bills on my back. I do not want to take bills in exchange for this gold." I can say, "Well, fill up a couple of gunny sacks of coins, get a wheelbarrow, and I will pay you in coin." He will say, "No, I don't want to go down the street wheeling a wheelbarrow full of coins."
Now, how else can I buy gold? Well, the legitimate way is to turn over the pages of a ledger, enter the number of his account at the top of the page, put down the date and credit his account with ten thousand units of account, or dollars, or the symbols we call dollars. And I can give him a little bankbook; I think I have one in my pocket. They cost us nothing.
I merely enter his name in this little bankbook which I have taken out of my drawer, and I enter in it the sum of $10,000-a perfectly legal procedure. There is nothing wrong with it. I have created this ten thousand units of account, or true dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: If what the hon. member says is true, why does he not sit down and write each one of us in the House of Commons a cheque for $10,000? We would all be rich then.
I can do that. But if we all did that, confusion would result. I say this is perfectly legitimate. There is nothing wrong with it. There is nothing wrong with these bills.
Send them over so that we can see.

And there is nothing wrong with our coin. There is nothing wrong with entering these units of account, or dollars, in this ledger. I am certain there are no people in the world who are greater experts on these matters than are the bankers themselves; and it is done every day in this manner.
I should like the Minister of Finance to give me a definite answer as to why the government does no>t go to the source for dollars, instead of impoverishing the people.

Before I could recommend that I would have to believe in my hon. friend's theories-which I do not. So that I am afraid what he suggests will not be brought into effect until his party is in power, and he is Minister of Finance.
I do not wish to limit the discussion, but I would recall to the attention of hon. members, through you Mr. Chairman, that we are dealing with an amendment to the Income War Tax Act which relates to permissible deductions from income. I wish to make only one comment, with respect to subsection I (e) (ii) (C):
(C) under twenty-one years of age and a student at a secondary school, university, or other educational institution.
I leave this suggestion with the minister; and I do not expect, of course, that he will carry it out this year. However I would expect the department to give it consideration. Let me point out that our universities and our higher educational establishments, despite the extraordinarily heavy enrolments which have taken place, are having a progressively more difficult time to make ends meet. I suggest to the department and the government that consideration be given to a direct deduction for secondary and higher education. I think that is important. The present situation is not peculiar to Canada but is happening all through the United States as well. Tuition fees are going up and almost every educational institution finds that its revenues are not sufficient to meet its charges. I would suggest that educational fees, fees paid for sons and daughters attending these educational institutions, be allowed as a deduction from income tax. I suggest that, not only because it is a good thing to encourage higher education, but because of the difficulties in which the universities find themselves. The university of Toronto, while its endowment is heavy, will face serious difficulties in the years to come in regard to higher education.
Do you include Rhodes scholars in that?
I would not be surprised-
Why?
Are you a Rhodes scholar?

Subsection 3 (iii) (B) reads:
(B) on underground development by a taxpayer operating a mine in a period of twelve months ending not later than the thirty-first day of December, 4950.
In that case one-half of the expenditures made during exploration is allowed. I suggest that here again one-half is not sufficient. I would ask that all the exploration charges be allowed as a deduction. I may be in error as to the exact intent of this clause, but it appears to me that here we have one-half of the expenditures made on underground development by a taxpayer developing a mine allowed as a deduction, and there are two or three things of which I believe the government is not fully aware. The United States experience- and they have suffered more or less in the same way as we have-is that not only are all the expenses of rehabilitating a mine allowed but that congress has passed an act actually bonus-ing a mine to get back into operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a special deferred maintenance provision. One-half can be charged back to a different period.
I appreciate that. This is not exploration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I mean is that this is a special provision in the law for deferred maintenance. The full cost of underground development by a taxpayer operating a mine can be taken at some time or another. This is a special provision given to taxpayers to make expenditures in a certain period, some time prior to 1950, and to charge half back to another period, say 1946, 1945 or 1944. The other half will presumably be charged in the year in which the expenditure is actually made.

Therefore, if a mine is badly behind in its development, as every mine with one or two exceptions is, and is able to get sufficient labour to catch up with its development and put its development into shape it can say in 1949 or 1950: We have spent so many thousands of dollars on back development work which we should have done in 1944 or 1945, and therefore we can take that development as a direct charge against the excess profits taxes we paid in 1944.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

And get a refund of the excess profits tax paid?

I had this out with the minister's predecessor and it was never quite clear just what the position was. Several properties paid royalties to the province and they were not allowed them as a deduction. I merely want to have it made absolutely 83166-252
clear that a royalty paid to the province is allowed as a tax deduction or allowed as an expense.

If a farmer employs casual labour is it still necessary for him to deduct the tax if the labourer is working at a rate that would bring him into the taxation bracket? Are the farmers supposed to deduct the tax and send it in?

speechtext: I believe that is correct; they are treated in the same way as any other man.

There is one other point I should like to take a minute or two on, because on his estimates the Minister of Agriculture said that it should be discussed when the income tax bills were before the committee, and this is a case where it is actually in order. The minister has made several statements pointing out that the deduction of S500 for the production of hogs and dairy products would really not work out as was suggested. On several occasions he said that the figures showed that only seven per cent of the farmers in Canada were paying taxes. That may be true in the general picture; but, according to the 1941 census, there were about
650,000	farmers in Canada. In 1945, some 27,411 farmers were assessed income tax. Out of those 27,411, 20,372 were from the three prairie provinces. Not many days ago we received another return showing that, out of 108 inspectors assessing farmers' income tax in Canada, seventy-nine were employed in the three prairie provinces, compared with twenty-nine in the other six provinces of Canada. The point I am coming to is that in these three prairie provinces for some reason there has been a great decrease in the production of hogs and of beef cattle. The other evening I asked the minister if he could tell us the position of beef cattle between the prairie provinces and the rest of Canada. I have the figures now for Canada in 1945, which was the last year I could get, showing 6,760,000 beef cattle in Canada. Of this number, 3,596,000

Income War Tax Act

beef cattle were in the three prairie provinces, again a greater number than in all the rest of Canada.
In the matter of hog production, the greatest year in history showed a total of some
8,863,000	hogs. Of this number, 5,768,000 odd were produced in the three prairie provinces. They have now practically gone out of hog production in the three prairie provinces. While the figures given by the Minister of Agriculture may be generally true of Canada as a whole, these figures give some idea of the great decrease in the production of essential foodstuffs, at least in the three prairie provinces. Yet for some reason or another the department has come to the conclusion that the inspectors should move into these particular provinces. I am not saying that they should not do that; probably they should do . it all over Canada, but I think it proves conclusively that in a very short period of time, for some reason, if not income tax-I think it certainly enters into the picture- we have lost the production of some millions of hogs in these three provinces.
The situation is not as set forth by the minister the other night that, in driving through Ontario and Quebec, one finds that in each of these provinces the bulk of the production came from places where you found two or three brood sows on the farm and maybe up to a dozen or twenty steers. That is not the situation. The bulk of the beef comes from the three prairie provinces, and in the years of heavy production the great majority of the hogs came from the three prairie provinces. I wanted to put that on the record to support the request which has been made by several hon. members that serious consideration be given to some further exemption for such production as that. On the facts I have given, one can say that the request was well taken and should be seriously considered. If these figures can be refuted I should be glad to hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not competent to discuss the reasons for the reduction in hog production in western Canada. I doubt whether it is due to the income tax law, although that may have some little effect on it, but I would say that it must be due to other causes. I dare say that on his estimates or at some appropriate time the Minister of Agriculture will deal with the subject.
I hope it will be in order at that time.

The Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue are the ones to deal with income tax. I believe that the hon. member for Souris is quite correct in the

statements he has made. These statements can be obtained from any number of farmers in my part of the country and from many others with whom I have come into contact in Ontario and in other parts as well. I believe that the Minister of Finance is the man who has to find the money to pay the country's bills. If he will not go to the proper sources for it, if he will not do what was suggested by the hon. member for Souris, then he is helping to cut down the production on Canadian farms.
How much money are you supposed to pay a hired man before he comes under the income tax brackets? Is there a stated amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It depends on whether he is married or single. It is all set out in the tables and I shall read it. If he is working a certain number of days which produces an income in the case of a single man in excess of $750 and in the case of a married man in excess of $1,500, taking into account the value of board and room and so on, then the deduction must be made.
If you are hiring the man only for a day or for a few days is it necessary to make the deduction? Is there a stated number of days that you must pay him before you take anything from him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The daily rate is set out in the new table. For a single man, the rate is $2.70 to $2.79 a day. If you pay a man that amount or in excess of that the table of deductions starts and it is at that rate. If he is a married man the wage- could be large without the requirement for a deduction. The income tax deduction tables, which are available in the Department of National Revenue, show the point at which it starts.
I understand that the deduction would start after you pay him over $2.79 a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he is a single man.

Is the minister aware that, in many cases, if a farmer tells his hired man that he is going to take income tax from him he puts on his coat and goes on to the next farm where he does not have to pay income tax. If the minister is not aware of that, how is he to take care of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I dare say that is true. There are a lot of people in this country-I suppose it is human nature-who do not like to pay taxes and who try to avoid paying them; but somebody has to pay them if they do not pay them. If the particular man that

Income War Tax Act
my hon. friend is referring to does not pay them somebody else has to pay the shot. We try to catch up with him; but, human nature being what it is and with the shortage of enforcement staff, of course we do not get them all. The fact of the matter is that there is a responsibility on every citizen of this country who gets the benefit of the country and the protection that the law affords to pay their proper share of the taxes. I have no sympathy for those who take advantage of one means or another to avoid the payment of taxes. That is what it is, evasion, and nothing else.
I am sorry I did not get in until quite late. Does the word "mine" here include an oil well? I am not speaking of deferred maintenance or anything like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the first time the question has been raised. I do not believe it does.
We get in through some other back door.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so, yes.

Keeping in mind the
exemptions in this section, I am interested in the reply that the minister gave to the hon. member for Edmonton East, namely, that the purpose of taxation was to provide revenue. I think he will admit that that is only part of the answer because, during the war, we were told that the main purpose of taxation was not merely to provide revenue but to curtail expenditure; in other words, to prevent inflation. I take it that in setting up this schedule the minister has in mind that the present rate of taxation is necessary in order to prevent inflation. The point I am interested in is this: If the situation that he pointed out in his budget speech develops whereby our income becomes lower, demand falls off and unemployment increases, then I should imagine it would be necessary to try to stimulate spending. The deputy minister of finance, Doctor Clark, made it quite clear and I quoted from his speech where he said that during the war the main purpose of maintaining heavy taxation was to curtail spending. Then, for exactly opposite reasons after the war it will be necessary to reduce taxation in order to expand spending. I take it that the present rate of taxation is the rate the department considers necessary to stabilize demand and supply. What will be the point when we reach the period which the minister envisaged in his speech where demand starts to lag? Will the government then still further 83166-252J
reduce taxation in order to encourage spending or, on the other hand, will they then be willing to create the money required to expand the purchasing power of the people? I think that is an interesting point.
I have in mind the fact that Mr. Graham Towers, during a broadcast on post-war finance, admitted that the time may come when demand falls off and for that reason it will not be desirable to increase taxation. We may have unemployment and it may be necessary to finance national projects. Obviously you could not finance those national projects by increased taxation because that would reduce still further your demand in relation to supply. Mr. Graham Towers admitted that, when that time comes, he would advocate the creation of money to finance worth-while projects. Would the minister agree that the present scale of taxation is not merely for the purpose of providing revenue but is for the purpose of maintaining a balance between demand and supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was very much interested in the observations of my hon. friend who has a good grasp of this question, but I do not think this is the proper time to discuss theories of taxation, the economic effects of taxation or the use of the income tax or any other tax as a fiscal weapon. I will content myself with saying that the primary purpose of taxation is to raise the necessary revenues to pay the current expenses of the country, to provide for the servicing of its national debt and, if possible, to reduce that debt. Of course it has an incidental effect in that it is a powerful fiscal weapon; it is an anti-inflationary weapon.
It is perfectly true that during the war we were spending a great deal of money and producing a great deal. Goods were being paid for but were not being consumed. In that case high taxes were a potent fiscal weapon in order to prevent inflation. However, I do not think this is the time to discuss these questions. We are on a specific section of the income tax act and I do not think this is relevant. On an appropriate occasion I shall be glad to debate and discuss these questions with my hon. friend on which, as I say, he has a wide and specialized knowledge, but I do not think this is the time.

In the past we have not considered it necessary to try to raise enough revenue by taxation to balance the budget, because in the eighty years since confederation we have had only sixteen balanced budgets. This shows that we have not considered it necessary to try to balance revenues with expenditures. Therefore I am wondering why at this time the government are not willing
Income War Tax Act

to raise the exemptions. I take it that the only reason the government are not prepared to raise the exemptions is that, if they do that, it will cause inflation. Naturally, when you increase the purchasing power in the lower income brackets you are creating a greater demand for goods than you could by increasing the purchasing power of any other class. It is the people in the lower income brackets who largely spend their incomes on goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I deny the statement of my hon. friend that the only purpose of maintaining the income tax at the present level is to prevent inflation; the purpose is to raise the necessary revenues to pay our bills this year and, while conditions are good, to make a reasonable contribution toward the reduction of the national debt. I am not one of those who believe that you can indulge in deficit financing year after year, although there may be years when it is necessary. I repeat that I do not intend to be drawn and I do not think I should be drawn into a discussion of these questions. If we are, there will be no end to it because there are a great .many other members who would like to voice their views. I suggest that it is not relevant to the section we are discussing.

On what
authority does the minister say that a drilled oil well is not a mine? Mines are used for the production of minerals and oil is classified as a mineral. When we reserve rights in the crown for mines and minerals we also reserve oil, the basis being that oil is considered a mineral. That may be wrong in fact; nevertheless that is the interpretation which the courts have given. I should like to know why the man who drills a small hole in the ground in order to get a mineral is any different from the man who digs a shaft as large as the aisle between us. They are both in the same position as far as I can see. There is no doubt that oil is a mineral and there should be no difference whether you dig a small shaft or a large one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be
perfectly right. So far as I am aware, this is the first time the question was raised and I just gave it my off-hand opinion. Perhaps an oil well is a mine.

Is the Department of
Finance or the Department of National Revenue doing anything with regard to the many requests which have come from agricultural bodies throughout the country asking that a broader interpretation be made of the regulations in order to make it possible for a farmer whose whole family is taking part in the production of a certain income not

to be the one against whom the whole income is assessed? I think there is a general realization that farming is different from ordinary business. The income tax forms are evidently made out to take care of the ordinary business operating from year to year. Farming is quite a different thing. Farmers and farm organizations have protested and urged that something be done. I understood the minister to say that something was being done and I should like to know if that is so. At the same time could he tell us if anything is being done to simplify tax forms for farmers. The T.l supplementary is quite simple and it can be filled out by most farmers who have any records at all. It seems to me that that would be quite sufficient for the large majority of farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The second part of my
hon. friend's question relates to the Department of National Revenue. As to members of a family working on a farm, the same position obtains there as with any other group. If a farmer's sons are working for him he can pay them wages and he can deduct those wages as an expense of his own.
If they are over sixteen years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have forgotten the
administrative rule. Of course, if he pays them too much he loses the benefit of the exemption which he is entitled to claim under the income tax act, of $300 in the case of a child over sixteen years. The same rule applies to the man with a business or store who has sons working for him.

If a man operating a business in town requires any help he hires it from other people around; they come in and assist him. I suppose it would be possible for his children to go and work for someone else. In the case of a good many farm families children of eight or nine years of age help feed the hogs and milk the cows. The wife on the farm helps in the production by milking the cows, taking care of chickens and working in the garden. The income earned by the woman in western Canada who raises a couple of hundred turkeys, hundreds of pounds of chickens, eggs and cream, is all placed on the one man. I understood the minister to say that something was being done about the matter, and I wanted to know what has been done or what has been contemplated. Then there is my other question about the simplification of the tax form.

If I understood the
minister correctly, he said that a farmer is entitled to pay wages to his son. It seems

Income War Tax Act
to me that I did hear him add, "And if he is over sixteen years of age, can claim exemption." Is that a fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He cannot claim both.
I wanted to be clear on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I have said, he cannot claim both.
In other words, if he pays his son wages in excess of the exemption, I gather that he cannot claim any exemption. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
I was not quite clear. I might have misunderstood the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
I should like an answer to the question raised by the hon. member for Yorkton with respect to the farmer's wife. Is there anything on that? Is there any relief?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course the same question comes up year after year. The farmer's wife is in the same position as a small storekeeper's wife who helps him in his store, or a man's wife who has a little garden at his home, who works in the garden, keeps chickens, and so on. It has never been felt, either by my predecessor or by myself, that a special income tax provision should be made for the farmer's wife as distinguished from other groups in the community.

There was another question I should like to ask the minister with reference to veterans and the exemption for students. In the case of a student under twenty-one years of age, the parent is exempted if he is supporting the student. As the minister knows, there were a good many young men of eighteen or nineteen years of age who were in the army for only one and a half or two years. They get their $60 a month, but they are now over twenty-one years of age, and are being supported at the universities by their parents. I think there should be a clause exempting the parent who is supporting those sons and daughters, and providing for the same exemption for them. The principle of exempting them under twenty-one is exactly the same principle as should apply in exempting them over twenty-one. Has any consideration been given to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, quite extensive consideration has been given to it. I dealt with
this matter at some length when we were at the resolution stage. I explained that the age limit of twenty-one was fixed with this idea in mind. That is the age at which, ordinarily, young people finish their arts course or their ordinary university course. If they are going on to take specialized professional training to become lawyers, engineers, or whatever it may be, it is felt that the income tax exemption for the parents should not continue beyond that age. In other words, it is felt that there should not be a special income tax exemption for those who are carrying on postgraduate studies. That does not run into very large figures. As my hon. friend will appreciate, a $300 exemption, with a taxation rate of twenty per cent, which carries one up to the type of income of something of the order of $5,000, is worth only $60 a year under the new schedule of tax rates, so that it is not a substantial proportion of the cost of education. The costs, of course, run very much more than that, and they must be found from other sources. So that if one takes the case of parents who are helping to send their children to university, in the average income group of $5,000 a year, which perhaps is putting it high, the tax value of that to the parent is, in any event, only $60 under the new act.
I was not speaking of the general application. I was speaking only of the young man who is in the army.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You had reference to
veterans.
Yes.

I do not intend to just ask a question here, and I do not intend to say anything on this section except what I wish to say right now. We are on section 4 of Bill No. 269, an act to amend the Income War Tax Act. This is a large section with a good many subsections, divisions, subdivisions and a few sub-subdivisions. The whole thing is on the matter of income tax, exemption and some details in administration. What I wish to say is this, and it is in respect to the two questions that were asked by the hon. member for Edmonton East and the hon. member for Acadia. These questions could have been asked on the resolution stage of the bill but we are always met with this reply, "Well, now, if you will wait until the bill comes down, I will be able to answer it then." By obliging the minister, we let the resolution pass and wait till the bill comes down. Surely, when we are discussing a section like this we should be able to ask the minister a few questions as to why all this income tax is necessary. The hon. member for Edmonton
Income War Tax Act

East asked, what is the purpose of this taxation? Why take it out of the people? Why not go to the very source from which money comes? The minister evaded that question

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. He answered it.
-by saying he did not want to get involved-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, he answered it, and answered it directly.

I will accept the
minister's statement, but I am quite confident that when he reads Hansard tomorrow he will find that it was not answered directly. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 4 as amended carry?

I am still confused about the situation with respect to the payment to a farmer's family in relation to farm produce. We have been given what I consider to be contradictory explanations in connection with this, and I should appreciate it very much if the minister would tonight give us an explanation which would stand up year after year. On some occasions we have been told that a farmer can pay his family without affecting the allowance as dependents. Again

we have been told we cannot do that. I should like very much to get a definite statement by which we can go from year to year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought I had given that answer a few minutes ago. I am told that the age is sixteen; apparently that is an administrative ruling.
Then children below sixteen can or cannot be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

What about the $100 exemption, now?

speechtext:
Did the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska have a question to ask?

I got my answer from the minister privately, and I am satisfied.

I am not going to take up very much time, but I want to say in the most kindly way and most constructive way that here as members of parliament, we are all interested in trying to do what is best for our country. We are attempting to discourage inflation and, at the same time, get production. I have been on a farm for twenty-five years, and no one knows better than I do what farmers' wives and families do in connection with the production of farm products. If we are to have the increased production we want, then we must discourage deflation. Nothing is more likely to keep the boys on the farm than to encourage them to make a little money on the side. Those boys who have been brought up on the farm, and at the ages of four or five years can drive horses, or at eight or nine years of age can drive tractors, are the ones who will make constructive farmers. If we have to depend upon some of these people from the city, then let me say that they do. more damage than they are worth. There is not?

JTbo Deputy Chairman.]

I have one more question for the minister to answer. We are getting more satisfactory answers tonight than we have ever been able to get before. The farmer's wife does all the work herself; the farmer does not have a thing to do with it. She receives the cheques and spends the money. What happens in a case of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Individual cases have to be considered on their merits. If the money she receives in proportion to the full income of the farm is not out of keeping with what she might have by way of pocket money, it is not taxable.

There is a principle there; I do not think it should come down to individual cases. If a principle were laid down we would know where we stand, because, as I said before, the imposition of this tax has considerably cut down production of cream, milk, butter and eggs.
I thought the subsections were to be called. If not, I should like to ask a question about section 4 (4). What is that order in council?

That is the order in council which fixes the period of twelve months commencing January 1, 1946, and terminating

Just one question with regard to subsection

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend will
appreciate, this is a concession which is given, not to a province, but to taxpayers who are subject to tax in a province on the same profits. In the agreements with the provinces with respect to taxation, which existed during the war, it became necessary to specify what were profits derived from mining operations or on income derived from logging operations. I believe the committee will appreciate that there is a difference between mining operations as such, and the processing of ore. There is a difference between revenues from logging operations and operations in connection with
the finishing of lumber. It is difficult to spell this out in a statute and, as is the case in a number of these situations, it is desirable to leave some latitude, some flexibility. But rather than leave it in the discretion of the minister, it was provided in the law that the condition would be fixed by the governor in council and would be known to all who are interested. It provides a more flexible way of amending the provisions, if they are found to be unsatisfactory.
I suggest that it might give rise to another kind of log-rolling.

I should like to speak
with respect to subsection 5, about which there has already been some discussion. What reference has this to matters under discussion between the dominion and the provinces? As I understand it, in the negotiations with reference to new tax agreements the position taken by the provinces was that they should have those six so-called minor fields of taxation yielded up to them exclusively, and that, in addition, they should have priority in the fields of mining and logging, because in that instance it was the development of natural resources which was being taxed, and for that reason they felt they should have priorities in those fields. Would the minister make a statement as to the relationship between this amendment in section 4 (5) and those matters that were under negotiation between the dominion and the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This provision permitting a deduction from income tax for this particular purpose applies whether or not a province enters into a taxation agreement with the dominion. Ordinarily the general rule is and always has been that, for purposes of dominion income tax, the taxpayer is not entitled to deduct profits tax, a tax in the nature of income tax paid to a provincial jurisdiction. There is an exception, however, in the case of mining and logging profits, and that applies whether or not a province enters into a taxation agreement with the dominion. In other words, all provinces are entitled to impose taxes on mining and logging profits, and those taxes may be deducted as an expense by the taxpayer as though they were an expense under the dominion income tax law. But in order to protect the dominion treasury in respect of this special deduction which is allowed for this type of income, it must be clearly income derived from logging and mining operations, and not income derived from processing operations, or income derived from manufacturing the logs, for
Income War Tax Act

instance, after they have been cut. The only purpose of this amendment is to make it clear that the profits tax or income tax imposed should be on the same income in each case, and not, for instance, on the income of a previous year, although paid in the same taxation year.

I thank the minister for his clear statement. Will he say to what extent the terms of this amendment go in meeting the views* of the provinces as set out in the negotiations? I gathered from the minister's statement that it goes a substantial way, but that there still remains a field perhaps in connection with processing where the demands of the provinces have not been fully met by the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not quite sure to what negotiations my hon. friend is referring.

I am referring to the position taken by the provinces a year ago in this building at the dominion-provincial conference, when they asserted their claim to the six minor taxation fields and priority in the fields of logging and mining. This amendment, I gather from the minister's statement, does go some way in recognizing the claim of the provinces to priority in mining and logging.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This amendment does not change the position at all. Paragraph (w) as contained in the law last year extended the principle that logging and mining profits taxes imposed by any province could be deducted from gross profits before computing dominion income tax. The amendment this year is a minor one to ensure that the profits tax will be calculated on the same set of profits, not on other profits.
In this subsection the term "mining operations" is a different expression from that used in subsection 3. I would ask the minister whether mining operations covers the drilling of an oil well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would have to give very much the same answer I gave in the other case. I do not believe it is. But if drilling an oil well is mining I suppose it would be covered.

Can the minister tell me why it is not? Drilling an oil well is clearly a mining operation. It cannot be anything else. It is going into the ground for minerals just as all mining is. 
'Mr. ABBOTT: I am told that no provincial government in Canada imposes any income tax on oil well companies. It all takes the form of a royalty, and that, of course, is clearly deductible. So that the question has not arisen as a practical one so far.
The minister is quite right about that. But let us look to the future. I live in a place where, if I may say so, with great respect, they may tax anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might encourage the imposition of a profits tax by provincial governments. I do not know whether we should do that or not.
I take it that the simple answer is this. The minister says that he does not know whether mining operations covers drilling for oil or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not believe it does.

My opinion is so contrary to his. Oil is a mineral and drilling for oil is a mining operation. You go into the ground to get it. Gold is a mineral and you go into the ground to get it. The only difference is the size of the hole you put down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is an expert on oil wells and I am not.

speechtext:
My experience, in my seven years in the house is that, during the course of a session, numerous occasions arise in which this matter is debated at length. When would the minister like to be engaged in such a discussion, because we shall be glad to suit his convenience?

speechtext: Order.

speechtext: I repeat again what I said before, that the question only has significance in the case of a profits tax being imposed by a provincial jurisdiction. But once something gets on the statute books and is interpreted, it stands that way. I agree with the minister that what they get is a royalty, in our province one of 12J per cent. The minister generously said that he allows them that, and I appreciate his generosity in that particular. Of course it is none of his business anyway because the province owns the resources. I am not suspicious of the minister; I am suspicious of the government of the province in which I live, and I should like the views of the minister perhaps a little more expertly directed than he has shown up to the moment as to why the drilling of an oil well is not a mining operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a question to which I would have to give the most careful consideration. I would hesitate to try to give a snap answer this evening.
I will accept that; I have been stalled quite often and I have become used' to it.
I have not yet received an answer to my question.
You never will.
Does the minister consider the production of oil from the tar sands of Alberta the same type of business as the production of oil from an oil well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a question I am not really competent to answer. The answer is the same one I gave to the hon. member. It has no practical significance, because I believe that there is no profits tax as such imposed by the province on the particular development to which my hon. friend refers, and I have never had to consider it.
You spent millions of your own money up there.
Is it true that there are only two provinces, namely the provinces which have not come into agreement with the dominion, which impose corporation profits tax on mining operations? Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I believe there are other provinces. I would have to check, although I am told that Saskatchewan has a type of taxation which is called a royalty, but which is, in fact, on a net basis.

I know the circumstances of that tax which operates on a particular property. The point I am making is purely and simply directed to exempt taxes paid by mining and logging companies which pay corporation profit taxes to the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily corporation profits taxes. This is profits tax or income tax on income derived from logging or mining operations, and it would not necessarily have to be a corporation; it could be an individual who has engaged in that type of work.
An individual engaged in cutting trees? I have never heard of a case like that. If he paid taxation it would be on a stumpage basis, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably it does not exist today; but suppose a provincial government imposed an income tax, as it is free to do. It could impose it on a man who was engaged in logging and mining operations. It would have to be a special tax imposed with respect to these two types of operation; but it would be clearly within the rights of a provincial government to impose such a tax. I do not know that they do now.
Therefore you are getting to this; you are exempting from double taxation mining and logging? That is the basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

Mining and logging are exempt from double taxation?
